newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-SAMPRAS SERVE SEES HIM THROUGH FIVE-SET DRAMA.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS SERVE SEES HIM THROUGH FIVE-SET DRAMA.

text.p: Chinks appeared in Pete Sampras's armour at Wimbledon on Wednesday, but he closed them in time to survive a 6-4 6-3 6-7 6-7 6-4 tussle with Petr Korda and reach the quarter-finals for the sixth year in succession.
The world number one looked to be cruising at 6-4 4-2 against the Czech, ranked 24 in the world, when bad light forced them off the court on Tuesday night.
When play resumed, he held his serve to take the second set, but Korda, who has won two five-set matches against the American in the past, stepped up a gear.
He defended his own serve solidly and attacked at the net, rattling the three-times Wimbledon champion.
Sampras, showing uncharacteristic fragility with a flurry of errors, threw away a 5-1 lead in the third-set tie-break.

He also failed to capitalise on two match points -- falling over as he was wrong-footed by the Czech on one and suffering a blistering cross court pass on the other. Korda, 29, eventually won the tie-break 10-8.
Sampras also appeared nervy in the second tie-break putting several shots that he would normally have placed to the centimetre, wide and long.
The American's shoulders dropped when he netted a volley to offer the Czech the set. Korda leapt in the air with a double scissor jump to celebrate.
But joy was short-lived. Sampras, whose own serve was not broken throughout the match, pounced and broke the Czech in a closely-fought first game.
"I was unlucky with two bad bounces," Korda said. "And he hit everything inside."
The three-times champion then sailed home on his serve, losing only two points in four service games.
"It was in my hands and I let it slip away a bit," Sampras said.
"I worked a lot harder than I would have liked," he added.
He thumped down an ace -- his 28th of the match -- to earn his last eight place.
"But I expect myself to win and that's the most important thing."
Sampras, the top seed and favourite here, had not lost a set in his first three rounds. But his recent tournament form has been patchy.
After a great start to the year with wins at the Australian Open, San Jose and Philadelphia he hit a knotty patch and his record is now 11 wins to seven defeats since.
He slumped out of the semifinals of the pre-Wimbledon Queen's event to unheralded Swede Jonas Bjorkman.
While he has an exceptional Wimbledon pedigree with a 33-2 match record, he will not be able to forget his quarter-final defeat last year to eventual champion Richard Krajicek.
Krajicek was beaten on Wednesday by Briton Tim Henman but Sampras meets another three-times winner in Boris Becker in the quarter-finals.
Sampras said the draw was hard for both men. "We've had some unbelievable matches," he said.
"Boris and I have a lot of respect for each other ... he is a class act."
Becker arrived a the quarter-finals with four straight sets victories and he has had a day off before the quarter-finals clash on Thursday.
Korda believes Sampras will find the going tough.
"He used a lot of energy today," Korda said "I think he is going to feel that tomorrow."
